Draft: a student report on a school project about conductors. Writer: Priya Vandermolen, junior at Halvern Ridge High, observed the Corlett Valley Youth Orchestra.

Sentences:
P1: [1] Conductors are interesting and there are many things to say about them. [2] For our music-history project, I spent three Thursday rehearsals watching Maestra Ilse Okonkwo-Dahl lead the Corlett Valley Youth Orchestra. [3] She is the only person on stage who makes no sound at all.
P2: [4] Before the first rehearsal, the principal cellist told me that musicians follow the conductor's breath more than her baton. [5] At the second rehearsal, I watched Okonkwo-Dahl inhale sharply before the opening chord of a Brahms-style overture the group was learning, and all forty players came in together. [6] When she did not breathe, the entrance was ragged.
P3: [7] Conductors always control everything that happens in a performance. [8] In the third rehearsal, Okonkwo-Dahl stopped the brass four times in ten minutes. [9] She never raised her voice, though. [10] She just lowered her left hand slowly, and the trumpets got softer, which was a thing that happened each time she did the hand thing, and it was pretty awesome to see.
P4: [11] In the end, conductors are a big deal.

Flaws: 1 vague thesis (4.B), 7 overstated (4.C), 6 lacks commentary after (6.A), 10 wordy/tone (8.A on "pretty awesome"; 8.B on 10 wordiness). Use 8.A on sentence 10's "pretty awesome" and 8.B... overlap; instead 8.A target sentence 9 "though"? Better: make 8.A target a separate sentence. Change sentence 9 to "The brass players were totally freaking out about it." Hmm, keep factual: [9] "Honestly, the brass section got kind of bossed around." Audience: teacher and classmates, formal report. 8.A replaces 9. 8.B revises 10 to "She simply lowered her left hand slowly, and each time, the trumpets softened." 2.A conclusion 11.

input.title: The Silent Player: Watching a Conductor at Work
paragraphs: Conductors are interesting and there are many things to say about them.
For our music-history project, I spent three Thursday rehearsals watching Maestra Ilse Okonkwo-Dahl lead the Corlett Valley Youth Orchestra.
She is the only person on the stage who makes no sound at all.
Before the first rehearsal, the principal cellist told me that the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton.
At the second rehearsal, I watched Okonkwo-Dahl inhale sharply just before the opening chord of the overture the group was learning, and all forty players came in together.
Later, when she forgot to breathe before the same chord, the entrance was ragged.
Conductors always control everything that happens in a performance.
In the third rehearsal, Okonkwo-Dahl stopped the brass section four times in ten minutes.
Honestly, the brass guys got kind of bossed around, but she never raised her voice.
She just lowered her left hand slowly, and the trumpets got softer, which was a thing that happened each time she did the hand thing, and it was pretty awesome to see.
In the end, conductors are a big deal.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 11 with a conclusion that sums up what her observations showed about how a conductor leads without making sound. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Over three rehearsals, I learned that a conductor's breath and hands can carry an orchestra.
options.label: correct
options.why: Draws together the breath evidence (paragraph 2) and the hand gesture evidence (paragraph 3) as the way she leads silently.

options.text: In the end, I think everyone should go and watch a youth orchestra rehearse.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Makes a recommendation rather than summing up what the observations showed.

options.text: Conductors have existed for centuries and have changed music history.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Sweeping historical claim the report never discusses.

options.text: The trumpets got softer each time Okonkwo-Dahl lowered her hand.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Repeats one detail and leaves out the breath findings.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 1 into a thesis that makes a claim requiring proof and previews the two kinds of silent signals the report goes on to discuss. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Though she makes no sound, a conductor leads through her breath and her hands.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim and previews breath (paragraph 2) and hands (paragraph 3).

options.text: A conductor is the person who stands in front of an orchestra with a baton.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a definition that needs no proof and previews nothing.

options.text: Conductors lead through their breath, which players follow more than the baton.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Previews only breath and leaves out the hand gestures in paragraph 3.

options.text: Conductors are fascinating people, and I learned a great deal about them.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Still vague; it makes no specific claim and previews nothing.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 7 so it qualifies the overstated claim while still introducing the conductor's control over the players in paragraph 3. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A conductor cannot play a note, but she can shape much of how the players sound.
options.label: correct
options.why: Limits the claim ('much of') and acknowledges the limit, while setting up her control over the brass.

options.text: Conductors completely control every note that each player in the orchestra makes.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Makes the overstatement stronger instead of qualifying it.

options.text: Conductors have almost no real influence over how a performance sounds.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Swings to the opposite extreme and contradicts sentences 8-10.

options.text: Some say conductors control everything, and I agree with them on this point.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Brings in a vague outside view and keeps the absolute claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how the two rehearsal moments support the cellist's claim in sentence 4. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The contrast suggests that the players were timing their entrance to her breath.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the together and ragged entrances to the claim that players follow her breath.

options.text: The overture was difficult, and the group rehearsed it many times that day.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds background and does not explain how the evidence supports the claim.

options.text: This proves that a baton is useless and conductors should stop using one.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Overreaches far beyond what two entrances can show.

options.text: The cellist had played with the orchestra for several years before that.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Supports the cellist's credibility, not the link between evidence and claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise the underlined portion of sentence 9 ("Honestly, the brass guys got kind of bossed around") so it fits the objective tone of a report for her teacher and classmates. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: She corrected the brass players repeatedly
options.label: correct
options.why: Neutral, precise, and suitably formal for a report.

options.text: The brass dudes totally got called out over and over
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Even more slangy than the original.

options.text: The poor, suffering brass players were mercilessly tormented
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Melodramatic and not objective.

options.text: She praised the brass players again and again
options.label: reversal
options.why: Changes the meaning; sentence 8 shows she was correcting them.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 10 so that it is concise and clearly shows that her gesture caused the same result each time. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Each time she slowly lowered her left hand, the trumpets softened.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concise; 'each time' plus the main clause clearly shows the repeated cause and effect.

options.text: She lowered her hand, and the trumpets, which happened each time, softened.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The misplaced 'which' clause makes it unclear what happened each time.

options.text: Her left hand was lowered slowly, the trumpets got softer every single time.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Comma splice, and the passive voice is wordy.

options.text: She lowered her left hand slowly, although the trumpets softened each time.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: 'Although' signals contrast rather than cause.

Insulting tone toward the very readers being asked to vote

input.title: Homework at the Garden Fence
paragraphs: Every Thursday evening this fall, a few cars have been parked along the fence of the Hollis Creek Community Garden with their engines off and their dome lights on.
Inside them are kids from up on Marrow Ridge doing homework, because the weak Wi-Fi from the garden shed reaches the gravel lot and their houses get no signal at all.
Internet is important for students these days.
My name is Tessa Lindqvist, and I was one of those kids last spring.
Our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not even load on a phone showing one bar.
My neighbor's son, Caleb, failed a chemistry quiz because the practice set timed out four times on his mother's hotspot.
Obviously, anyone who doesn't get this is clueless about how school works now.
The garden committee could fix part of this problem cheaply.
A signal booster mounted on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, according to the hardware co-op in Pell.
A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car.
The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed.
Some members worry that teenagers will trample the beds or leave trash behind.
Students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night.
I am asking every member to vote yes at the November 9 meeting.

items.stem: Many garden members are retirees who keep a close eye on the committee's small budget. The writer wants to revise sentence 9 to address this audience's concern about cost. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, less than last summer's new hoses, and my family has offered to pay half.
options.label: correct
options.why: Puts the cost in terms members know and reduces the burden on the budget, directly answering their concern.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, which is honestly nothing compared to what a good education is worth.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dismisses the members' budget worry instead of addressing it.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof, a model with two antennas and a weatherproof case, is sold at the hardware co-op in Pell.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds product details but drops the cost entirely, ignoring the audience's concern.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, and it would probably pay for itself many times over someday.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a vague, unsupported financial claim that does not reassure budget-minded readers.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 5 that respects members who finished school without the internet while explaining why students today cannot do the same. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, but today the assignments themselves exist only online.
options.label: correct
options.why: Honors members' experience and explains the change that makes their approach impossible now.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, which shows that the old way was always better for kids.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Undercuts the writer's own argument instead of explaining why students now need internet.

options.text: Many of you probably think kids today are lazy and just want to sit on their phones at the garden fence.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Assumes the worst of readers rather than respecting them, and explains nothing.

options.text: Today the assignments exist only online, and the school stopped handing out printed packets two years ago.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Explains the change but does not acknowledge members who studied without the internet.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that makes an arguable claim and previews the proposal developed in the rest of the flyer. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: With a cheap signal booster and a study table at the shed, our garden can give ridge students a safe place to do homework.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes a debatable position and previews the booster, the table and the vote-worthy proposal.

options.text: Students in rural areas across the country have trouble getting internet access at home.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: A general fact needing little proof; it does not preview the garden proposal.

options.text: The math program our teachers use will not load on a phone that shows only one bar.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: A single supporting detail, not a claim governing the whole flyer.

options.text: Some people say the garden should help students, and others say it should stick to growing food.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Reports two views without taking a position or previewing the proposal.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition that signals a second, separate improvement following the one described in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: In addition,
options.label: correct
options.why: Signals that the table is a further improvement added to the booster.

options.text: In contrast,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals opposition, but the table complements the booster.

options.text: As a result,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly implies the booster causes the table to exist.

options.text: For instance,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Presents the table as an example of the booster, which it is not.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 13 with a transition that shows the sentence is a response to the worry raised in sentence 12. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: To address that concern,
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly marks sentence 13 as the answer to the members' worry.

options.text: Similarly to that concern,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals likeness, but sentence 13 answers rather than resembles the worry.

options.text: Because of that concern,
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Mentions the concern but frames the promise as merely caused by it, not as a reply.

options.text: Despite that small concern,
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Belittles the members' worry and suggests the writer will disregard it.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 7 with a sentence that keeps a respectful tone toward the garden members being asked to vote while stressing how serious the problem is. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For students on the ridge, a weak signal can mean the difference between passing and failing.
options.label: correct
options.why: Stresses the stakes without insulting the readers.

options.text: Seriously, it is kind of ridiculous that nobody around here has bothered to notice this yet.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Casual and accusatory toward the audience.

options.text: Such occurrences may, in certain instances, be regarded as somewhat inconvenient for pupils.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Stiff and understated, so it weakens the sense of seriousness.

options.text: Caleb later retook the chemistry quiz at school and earned a much better grade on it.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Polite, but it adds a new fact that makes the problem seem less serious.

content.text:
Draft plan: student editorial in the school paper of a fictional school urging students to join the volunteer trail crew. 4 paragraphs, about 260 words.

Writer: Priya Halvorsen, junior at Calder Ridge High School, writing for the "Ridgeline Courier." The occasion is the spring crew day on the Tamsett Trail, a fictional trail of 140 miles.

Sentences:
P1
1 Most people who hike the Tamsett Trail never think about who put the trail there.
2 The 140-mile path that crosses the hills above our town was not carved by nature or by a government agency.
3 It was built, and is still kept open, by volunteers with shovels.
P2
4 Building a trail is slower than most people imagine.
5 A crew first flags a route with orange ribbon, choosing a line that climbs gently so rain will not turn the path into a creek.
6 Then they cut back brush, dig out the tread with heavy hoes called pulaskis, and set stone steps where the slope is too steep.
7 Last October, a crew of twelve spent an entire Saturday finishing just forty feet of trail near Bramble Gap.
P3
8 Maintenance never ends. (flaw: missing transition, 6.B target at 9)
9 Every winter, storms knock trees across the path and wash out the drainage ditches the crews dug.
10 The Tamsett Trail Association says it needs at least sixty volunteers each spring to clear the damage.
11 Last year only thirty-one showed up. (4.A slot after 11 — evidence for the claim that the shortfall hurts the trail)
P4
12 Honestly, if you're not out there you're kind of being lazy, so get off the couch. (tone flaw, 8.A)
13 The spring crew day is April 19, volunteers meet at the Ridge Road trailhead at 8 a.m. (comma splice, 8.C)
14 Gloves, tools, and lunch are provided.

That's 14 sentences. Word count is roughly 230, which is fine.

Questions:
1. 2.B: the audience is classmates worried they have no experience. Add a sentence after 14. Key: "No experience is needed; crew leaders spend the first hour teaching newcomers how to use each tool safely." Distractors: a history of the association (off-audience), a sentence aimed at experienced builders, and one that insults beginners.
2. 4.A: after 11, support the claim that the shortfall has consequences. Key: "As a result, a two-mile stretch below Corbin Ridge stayed blocked by fallen trees until August." Distractors: a pleasant view (topic but not claim), hikers' numbers rising, and an unsupported general statement.
3. 6.B: the transition at the start of 9, the relationship being explanation/elaboration after 8. Key "Even after a trail is finished," at the start of 9 links 8 to P2. Better: revise sentence 8 to transition from building to maintaining. Key: "Finishing a trail, however, is only the beginning, because maintenance never ends." Distractors: "For example,..." (wrong relation), "Similarly..." (illogical), and "As a result of building being slow, ..." (wrong cause).
4. 6.C: the writer wants to help readers who have never seen trail work picture how slow the progress at 7 is, using a comparison. Key: "That is roughly the length of our school's hallway outside the cafeteria—about one day of work for twelve people." Distractors: comparing to other trails' length, a definition of pulaski (already given), and an anecdote of a hike.
5. 8.A: replace 12 to keep an urgent but respectful tone. Key: "The trail depends on people like us, and a single Saturday of work makes a real difference."
6. 8.C: fix 13. Key: "April 19; volunteers". Distractors: a comma splice kept with "and" missing, "April 19 volunteers" (run-on), and "April 19, and, volunteers" (misplaced commas).

The cognitive levels are mixed. I'll write it out.

blueprint.theme: how long-distance walking trails are built and maintained by volunteers

planned_flaws.flaw: abrupt shift from building to maintenance with no transition
statistic about the volunteer shortfall given without its consequence
forty feet is abstract for readers who have never seen trail work
insulting, flippant tone toward the audience
comma splice
conclusion does not address newcomers' worry about having no experience

input.title: Who Holds Up the Trail?
paragraphs: Most people who hike the Tamsett Trail never think about who put the trail there.
The 140-mile path that crosses the hills above our town was not carved by nature or by a government agency.
It was built, and is still kept open, by volunteers with shovels.
Building a trail is slower than most people imagine.
A crew first flags a route with orange ribbon, choosing a line that climbs gently so rain will not turn the path into a creek.
Then they cut back brush, dig out the tread with heavy hoes called pulaskis, and set stone steps where the slope is too steep.
Last October, a crew of twelve spent an entire Saturday finishing just forty feet of trail near Bramble Gap.
Maintenance never ends.
Every winter, storms knock trees across the path and wash out the drainage ditches the crews dug.
The Tamsett Trail Association says it needs at least sixty volunteers each spring to clear the damage.
Last year only thirty-one showed up.
Honestly, if you're not out there you're kind of being lazy, so get off the couch.
The spring crew day is April 19, volunteers meet at the Ridge Road trailhead at 8 a.m.
Gloves, tools, and lunch are provided.

items.stem: The writer knows that many classmates hesitate to volunteer because they have never done outdoor work. She wants to add a sentence after sentence 14 that addresses this worry directly. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: No experience is needed, because crew leaders spend the first hour teaching newcomers to use each tool safely.
options.label: correct
options.why: Speaks directly to inexperienced students' worry and reassures them with a concrete detail about training.

options.text: The Tamsett Trail Association was founded decades ago by a small group of hikers from three nearby towns.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives background history and does nothing to address newcomers' lack of experience.

options.text: Experienced builders should bring their own pulaskis, since the best tools always go to the earliest arrivals.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Speaks to experienced volunteers instead of the hesitant beginners the writer wants to reach.

options.text: Anyone who has never held a shovel will probably slow the crew down, but they are still welcome to come along.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Confirms the beginners' fear instead of reassuring them, so it would discourage the target audience.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that gives evidence the volunteer shortfall actually harmed the trail. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: As a result, a two-mile stretch below Corbin Ridge stayed blocked by fallen trees until the middle of August.
options.label: correct
options.why: Shows a specific, concrete consequence of the shortfall, supporting the claim that too few volunteers hurt the trail.

options.text: The volunteers who did come cleared the overlook at Bramble Gap, where hikers can see four counties on a clear day.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Describes work that got done, which suggests the shortfall did little harm.

options.text: The number of hikers using the trail on summer weekends has grown steadily over the past several years.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Relates to the trail in general but gives no evidence of damage caused by the missing volunteers.

options.text: Everyone knows that a trail without enough volunteers will eventually fall apart and disappear completely.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: An overstated generalization with no specific evidence of actual harm.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it moves clearly from the discussion of building the trail in paragraph 2 to the discussion of maintenance in paragraph 3. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Finishing a section of trail, however, is only the beginning, because maintenance never ends.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the finished construction in paragraph 2 to the ongoing maintenance in paragraph 3 and signals the shift with a contrast.

options.text: For example, finishing a section of trail is only one task, because maintenance never ends.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Says 'for example,' but maintenance is a new stage, not an example of building.

options.text: Similarly to building, which is very slow, maintenance of the trail never ends.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Treats slowness and endlessness as parallel ideas, so it misstates the relationship and the wording is awkward.

options.text: Because building is so slow and difficult, maintenance of the trail never ends.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly says slow building causes endless maintenance; storms cause it, as sentence 9 explains.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a comparison after sentence 7 that helps readers who have never done trail work picture how little forty feet is. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: That is about the length of the hallway outside our cafeteria, a walk that takes most of us ten seconds.
options.label: correct
options.why: Compares forty feet to a familiar school space, so readers can feel how small one full day's progress is.

options.text: A pulaski is a tool with an axe blade on one side and a digging blade on the other side.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Defines a tool instead of making the distance concrete, and sentence 6 already introduces the pulaski.

options.text: Other long trails in the region are even longer than the Tamsett, some stretching hundreds of miles.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Compares whole trail lengths, which does nothing to make forty feet of progress vivid.

options.text: I hiked that section myself in November and noticed how smooth and even the new path felt underfoot.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Adds a personal detail about the section but does not help readers grasp the small size of forty feet.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that it urges classmates to volunteer with an encouraging, respectful tone. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The trail depends on people like us, and a single Saturday of our work can make a real difference.
options.label: correct
options.why: Urges action respectfully and includes the writer among the readers, which suits an appeal to classmates.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who skips crew day is just proving they care more about their phones than about anything real.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insults the readers, keeping the hostile tone the revision is supposed to remove.

options.text: Participation in volunteer maintenance activities is hereby recommended to all members of the student body.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Stiff and bureaucratic, it sounds like an official notice instead of an encouraging appeal from a peer.

options.text: Maybe come if you feel like it, though it is totally fine if you would rather sleep in that Saturday.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Friendly, but it undercuts the urgency the editorial needs after the shortfall it has just described.

items.stem:
In sentence 13 (reproduced below), the writer wants to correct the punctuation between the two independent clauses.

The spring crew day is April 19, volunteers meet at the Ridge Road trailhead at 8 a.m.

Which choice should replace "April 19, volunteers"?

options.text: April 19; volunteers
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.

options.text: April 19 volunteers
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Creates a fused sentence with no punctuation between the independent clauses.

options.text: April 19, and, volunteers
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The comma after 'and' is incorrect and interrupts the conjunction from its clause.

options.text: April 19, so volunteers,
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Adds an illogical causal 'so' and puts an incorrect comma between the subject and the verb.

blueprint.purpose: To announce the library's annual Transfer Night and persuade adult readers, especially those returning to school, that community college transfer pathways offer a real second chance
blueprint.audience: Patrons of a small-town public library, including adults who left school early and parents of college-bound teenagers
blueprint.claim: Transfer pathways turn community college into a reliable route to a four-year degree, so readers considering a second start should come to Transfer Night
blueprint.theme: community college transfer pathways and the idea of a second chance

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that does not preview the post's argument or require proof
Comma splice joining two independent clauses
Wordy, vague, overly casual definition of transfer pathways
Abstract definition lacks a clarifying comparison for unfamiliar readers
Does not address readers who see community college as a lesser fallback
Flat, offhand conclusion that gives no invitation, details, or return to the second-chance idea

provenance.note: Fictional draft; all names, places and institutions invented.

input.title: Draft: Why Transfer Night Matters
paragraphs: Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there.
Community college is a good thing for a lot of people.
Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.
Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop.
At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University.
An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept.
He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.
Arturo's story is not unusual.
Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else.
Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important.
Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.
Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about.
Hope to see you there.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 12 with a closing sentence that invites readers to attend and returns to the idea of a second chance introduced through Arturo's story. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Bring your transcripts on April 17, and you might leave the way Arturo did, with your own second start folded in your pocket.
options.label: correct

input.title: Forty Lengths at Harrow Street
paragraphs: Every summer since I was fourteen, I have spent my mornings at the Harrow Street Pool in Calder Falls, first as a swimmer and now as a lifeguard.
Pools are important to communities in many ways.
At six in the morning, the lap lanes belong to retirees like Mr. Okafor, who swims exactly forty lengths and then tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself.
By noon, the shallow end fills with day-camp kids whose counselors call out names in four languages.
The pool brings together people who would never otherwise meet.
Last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from the apartments on Delmont Avenue how to float on her back, his hand flat beneath her spine until she no longer needed it.
Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street to save money.
Everyone in town agreed that this was a terrible idea.
I spoke at the budget hearing, holding a petition with 312 signatures I had collected at the snack bar.
The council kept the pool open, but it cut the evening hours, the only time many working parents could bring their children.
That decision was totally lame, and honestly it bugged me a lot.

What I learned from all of this is that the thing I learned is that a public space only stays public if the people who use it are willing to show up and speak up for it in the places where the decisions about it get made.
In conclusion, swimming is a very good form of exercise for people of all ages.

input.title: An Open Letter to the Marrick Hollow School Board Concerning the Thursday Design Lab
paragraphs: We are writing to you as the volunteers who have run the Thursday Design Lab at Marrick Hollow Middle School for the past four years, and we are writing because your agenda for the November meeting lists the Lab under "recreational programs proposed for discontinuation."
We understand the logic.

A line item that reads "game design" sits uneasily beside "algebra support" and "reading intervention" when the district must find 140,000 dollars in savings, and nobody on this board was elected to protect dice.

But we would ask you to consider that the word "game" is doing some misleading work on that agenda, and that what the Lab actually teaches is the one habit of mind the rest of the curriculum struggles hardest to deliver.

That habit is usually called systems thinking: the practice of seeing a situation not as a pile of separate facts but as a set of parts that push on one another, so that a change in one place shows up, often disguised, somewhere else.
Textbooks describe it.
Few of them let a thirteen-year-old feel it.
Playing a game does not quite do it either; a player learns the rules the way a passenger learns a road, by being carried over it.
Designing a game is different, because the designer must build the road, watch where it floods, and decide what to do about the water.
Consider what happened to a seventh grader we will call Dario, who spent six Thursdays building a trading game about a fishing village.
He gave each player a boat, a market and a simple rule: fish sold for two coins, and a second boat cost ten.
By the third round of his first playtest, one classmate owned four boats, the fish were gone, and the other players had nothing to do but watch.
Dario was furious, then puzzled, then quiet.
He had not written a rule that said "the rich get richer," yet his game had produced one on its own, and he had to work out why.
Over the next two weeks he tried a tax, then a spawning limit, then a recovery rule for empty waters, and each repair moved the problem rather than removing it.
What he finally understood, and could explain to the room, was that his village had a feedback loop in it, and that every honest fix would cost someone something.
No worksheet on ecology had ever gotten that far with him.
We would gently point out that the document in front of you is itself a system of exactly this kind.

Cut the Lab, and the forty students who attend it do not disappear; they go somewhere, and the district will pay for wherever that is, in supervision hours, in a crowded homework room, or in the slower currency of disengagement.
A budget, like Dario's village, is full of rules nobody wrote down.
Is it really more prudent to pull one piece out and hope the rest holds still?
We will not pretend that every child who leaves the Lab becomes an engineer, or even that every child who attends is building anything more ambitious than a card game about cats.
Some of them are.
But the cat game, too, has an economy, and its designer still has to answer the same question Dario answered: what happens to the whole when I change this part?
That question is the entire content of the course, and it travels well, into chemistry, into civics, into the student's own understanding of why a Tuesday went wrong.
We are not asking for new money.
We are asking that you move one line, from "recreation" to "instruction," and let the Lab be judged by what it teaches rather than by what it is called.
We will be at the meeting, with Dario's village and a set of boats, and we would be glad to let the board play a round.
We suspect you will find it familiar.

options.label: correct

options.why: The sentence affirms students who are ambitious; sentence 24 then defends even the cat game, so no frustration with trivial projects is expressed.

blueprint.speaker: Dell Hartigan, a retired bookbinder and parent volunteer who has run a monthly book swap at Corbett Hollow Middle School for five years
blueprint.audience: Parents and townspeople of Corbett Hollow who read the community newsletter, including some who watch school board decisions and some who regard the swap as a trivial stopgap
blueprint.exigence: The fifth anniversary of the swap, arriving as the school board prepares to vote again on the library budget
blueprint.purpose: To reframe the swap as a craft with its own lessons, to insist that it is not a substitute for a funded library, and to argue that it teaches children a habit of giving books that will outlast the budget vote
blueprint.context: Six years earlier the district cut the library purchasing allowance and reduced the librarian to part time; the writer began the swap in response
blueprint.claim: The book swap is best understood not as charity or as a replacement for the library but as a craft whose slow practice teaches children to pass books along, a habit that will outlast whichever way the budget vote goes
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 narrates the first swap and names the thesis (craft, not charity). Paragraph 2 supplies the exigence: the budget cut and its slow effect. Paragraph 3 asks what a swap does and answers with the handling: sorting, mending, keeping a ledger, and the lesson of slowness. Paragraph 4 concedes what the swap cannot do and refuses to let the board use it as an excuse. Paragraph 5 pivots to the one thing the swap does that the library never did: it makes givers of books, illustrated by an anecdote. Paragraph 6 qualifies the scale of the swap, then closes with the antithesis that a craft need not be large to be serious and that the habit will outlast the vote.

input.title: Take One, Leave One
paragraphs: The first swap, five Octobers ago, fit on two folding tables borrowed from the cafeteria at Corbett Hollow Middle School.
I brought forty-one books from my own shelves, most of them paperbacks with cracked spines, and a sign made from the back of a cereal box that said, in marker, Take One, Leave One, No Questions.
By the end of the lunch period the tables held fifty-three books, which is to say the children had done the arithmetic in our favor without being asked.
I have been running the swap every month since, and I have come to think of it less as a charity than as a craft, something with its own tools and its own slow lessons.
The reason the swap exists is not mysterious.

When the district trimmed its budget six years ago, the library's purchasing allowance fell from roughly nine thousand dollars a year to just over one thousand, and the librarian, Mrs. Avendale, went from full time to two days a week.
A thousand dollars buys perhaps sixty new hardcovers, in a building with four hundred and ten students.
The shelves did not empty overnight; they simply stopped growing, the way a town stops growing when the last factory closes and nobody notices until the graduating class is half its old size.
New titles arrived in children's conversations but not in the catalog, and the gap between what they wanted to read and what they could find became a kind of quiet weather in the building.
So what, exactly, does a book swap do that a shelf of donations in the front office does not?
The answer is in the handling.
Every month I sort what comes in, mend what can be mended with linen tape and a bone folder, and set aside what is beyond saving for the art teacher, who turns the pages into collage.
I keep a ledger, a spiral notebook, nothing grand, in which I write down what left the table and what came back.

The ledger has taught me more about the reading life of this town than any survey could: which series travel in packs, which single battered copy has passed through nine households, which eighth grader keeps bringing in horse novels she has outgrown so that someone younger can have them.
Mending is slow.
Sorting is slow.
That slowness is the point, because a craft is a thing you learn by doing it badly for a long time, and the children who help me have learned it alongside me.
I should be honest about what the swap cannot do.
It cannot buy the new book everyone is talking about; it can only wait for someone to tire of it.
It cannot catalog, cannot teach a sixth grader to find a source, cannot do the hundred invisible things Mrs. Avendale does in her two days.
A table of secondhand paperbacks is not a library, and anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse.
I would rather the board restore the budget tomorrow and put me out of business.
And yet.
There is one thing the swap does that the library, even in its funded years, never quite did: it makes children into givers of books rather than only borrowers of them.
A borrowed book is returned because it must be; a swapped book is released because somebody decided another reader should have it.

I have watched a boy stand at the table for most of a lunch period deciding whether he could part with a dog-eared fantasy novel, and I have watched him come back the next month to ask whether anyone took it.
Someone had.
He seemed, if anything, pleased, the way you are pleased to hear that a letter arrived.
I do not want to make the swap sound larger than it is.
It is two tables and a notebook and a roll of linen tape, and on a bad month it is forty books and a rainy lunch period.
But a craft does not have to be large to be serious, and a town does not have to be rich to teach its children that books are things you pass along rather than things you wait to be given.
The budget may come back; I hope it does.
The habit, I suspect, will outlast whichever way the vote goes.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's statement that "A table of secondhand paperbacks is not a library" most likely matters to the intended audience because it

options.text: assures readers who want the budget restored that the writer is not offering the school board a cheap substitute for funding
options.label: correct
options.why: The sentence continues that anyone who says otherwise 'is handing them an excuse,' and the next sentence wishes the board would restore the budget; the concession protects a shared interest of readers who want funding back.

options.text: reassures readers that the writer's mending and sorting are done with modest, inexpensive tools
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The tools appear in paragraphs 3 and 6, but this sentence concerns the swap's relation to the library and the board, not the cost of its tools.

options.text: signals to readers that the writer now doubts whether the swap has accomplished anything worthwhile
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 5 immediately asserts a benefit the swap uniquely provides; the concession limits the claim without abandoning it.

options.text: appeals to board members' expertise in budgeting by deferring to their judgment on library purchases
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage addresses newsletter readers, not board members, and never defers to the board's judgment; it warns against giving the board an excuse.

items.stem: The account of the boy and the "dog-eared fantasy novel" in paragraph 5 is likely to be persuasive to the newsletter's readers primarily because it

options.text: shows a change in a child's disposition that parents and neighbors can recognize without relying on figures
options.label: correct
options.why: The anecdote illustrates the claim in the preceding sentence that the swap makes 'givers of books'; the boy's hesitation and later pleasure make that abstract claim concrete for an audience of parents and townspeople.

options.text: demonstrates that the swap has increased the number of books circulating through the school each month
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The anecdote concerns one boy's decision to give a book away and his reaction; it says nothing about monthly circulation counts.

options.text: evokes sympathy for a child who was forced to give up a book he was not ready to part with
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The boy chose to release the book and 'seemed, if anything, pleased'; the anecdote conveys quiet satisfaction, not loss.

options.text: proves that the writer's mending with linen tape keeps even worn books in usable condition for years
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Mending belongs to paragraph 3; the dog-eared novel is mentioned to show the boy's attachment, not the writer's repair skill.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.text: The budget cut has quietly stalled the library's growth, leaving a gap between what students want to read and what they can find
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This summarizes paragraph 2's context, which establishes the exigence rather than the thesis about the swap as a craft.

options.text: The swap is best understood not as charity but as a craft whose slow practice teaches children to pass books along
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 4 states the swap is 'less a charity than a craft' with 'slow lessons,' and sentence 31 completes the claim that a town can 'teach its children that books are things you pass along.'

options.text: A monthly swap run by volunteers can adequately replace the services a funded school library once provided
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 4 explicitly denies this: 'A table of secondhand paperbacks is not a library,' and the writer wants the budget restored.

options.text: The school board should restore the library's purchasing allowance so that the librarian can return to full time
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer does hope the budget returns, but this is a wish expressed in passing; the essay's argument concerns what the swap is and what it teaches.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 4 and paragraph 5?

options.text: Paragraph 4 concedes the swap's real limits, and paragraph 5 identifies a distinct benefit that survives those limits
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 lists what the swap 'cannot do'; paragraph 5 opens 'And yet' and names 'one thing the swap does that the library... never quite did.'

options.text: Paragraph 4 raises objections from the school board, and paragraph 5 refutes each objection with evidence from the ledger
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The limits in paragraph 4 are the writer's own admissions, not the board's objections, and paragraph 5 cites an anecdote, not the ledger.

options.text: Paragraph 4 states the writer's claim about giving, and paragraph 5 retells that claim through a single narrative example
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The claim about giving appears in paragraph 5 itself, not paragraph 4; paragraph 4 is a concession, not a statement of the claim.

options.text: Paragraph 4 argues that the budget must be restored, and paragraph 5 supplies the reason the board has resisted doing so
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Paragraph 5 says nothing about the board's reasons; it describes what the swap does for children.

items.stem: The primary function of paragraph 2 within the passage as a whole is to

options.text: establish the circumstances that prompted the swap before the writer turns to what the swap actually does
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph opens 'The reason the swap exists is not mysterious' and recounts the budget cut and its effects; paragraph 3 then asks what the swap does.

options.text: argue that the district acted carelessly when it reduced the librarian to two days a week
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph reports the cut and its effects in a somber tone but does not accuse the district of carelessness or assign blame.

options.text: introduce the writer's central claim that the swap should be regarded as a craft rather than a charity
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: That claim is introduced at the end of paragraph 1; paragraph 2 provides context, not the thesis.

options.text: provide evidence that the swap has restored growth to shelves that had stopped expanding
options.label: reversal
options.why: The paragraph describes stalled shelves and a persistent gap; it does not claim the swap reversed the decline.

items.stem: The two-word sentence "And yet." at the beginning of paragraph 5 primarily serves to

options.text: halt the accumulating list of limitations and mark the writer's turn toward what the swap uniquely offers
options.label: correct
options.why: After four sentences of 'cannot' and a wish to be put out of business, the abrupt fragment pivots to 'one thing the swap does that the library... never quite did.'

options.text: express the writer's growing exasperation with a school board that has ignored repeated requests for funding
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Nothing in the surrounding sentences conveys exasperation; the fragment introduces a quietly affirming claim about children as givers.

options.text: condense the concessions of the previous paragraph into a brief summary before the essay's closing section
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The fragment does not summarize; it contrasts with what precedes it and opens a new line of argument, not the conclusion.

options.text: reveal the writer's lingering uncertainty about whether the swap accomplishes anything the library could not
options.label: reversal
options.why: The very next sentence states with confidence that there is 'one thing the swap does' the library never did; the fragment signals assertion, not doubt.

blueprint.speaker: Teodor Brandvik, a longtime columnist for the fictional Harrow County Ledger who knew Lenore Quist personally
blueprint.audience: Residents of Pell's Landing and the surrounding county who read the paper and, in many cases, donated to Lenore's fundraising page
blueprint.exigence: The death of Lenore Quist, a beloved school bus driver, after a widely shared medical crowdfunding campaign raised 53,400 dollars; the town is celebrating the figure, and the columnist feels the celebration hides an uncomfortable truth
blueprint.purpose: To honor Lenore sincerely while arguing that the success of her campaign, set beside a neighbor's failed one, exposes a system that rations care by popularity, and to redirect the readers' generosity toward a demand for structural change
blueprint.context: An obituary-style tribute column in a small-town newspaper, written within a week of the death, addressed to a community that regards the fundraising total as a point of pride
blueprint.claim: Crowdfunding gave Lenore real money and real comfort, but a system in which the sick must audition for survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to neighbors, and the community's kindness should not be mistaken for justice
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: P1 establishes Lenore's character through concrete anecdote and sets up the tension between honoring the figure and telling the truth. P2 narrates the campaign's success and the warmth behind it. P3 shifts tone and introduces the contrasting case of Aurelio Dansk, whose nearly identical situation raised almost nothing, isolating popularity as the deciding variable. P4 concedes the real benefits of the page, then rebuts with the lifeboat/harbor metaphor and the central claim about outsourced stinginess. P5 supplies the charity/justice distinction that explains why confusing the two makes the Aurelios invisible. P6 returns to direct address, asking donors to remember both Lenore and the fact that the burden should never have fallen on them.

devices.function: Opens with concrete details of Lenore's care for children to establish her character and the writer's firsthand knowledge
The colon introduces the town's ritual responses, ending pointedly on checking the fundraising figure
A long sentence of accumulated town rituals followed by the bare fragment of the dollar figure gives the number weight and ambiguity
The two fundraising totals, 53,400 dollars versus 1,100 dollars, are the comparative core of the argument
Narrates the campaign's creation and success to show the warmth it generated before the writer complicates it
The colon sets off the donor's note so that its plain words land with maximum pathos
The note about waiting in the snow and the image of opening the page before the pill organizer make the comfort of the campaign emotionally real
Shifts from elegiac tribute to pointed critique, signaling that the column will not be a conventional eulogy
Sets Aurelio's nearly identical case beside Lenore's to isolate being known as the variable that determined the money
The parallel gerund phrases (being known, being photographed well, having driven) make the criteria for deserving sound arbitrary and uncomfortable
The arithmetic of charity is pitiless, giving the impersonal system a cold agency
Grants the defenders' point that the money and comfort were real, then pivots with the lifeboat metaphor to the central claim
Lifeboat versus harbor distinguishes emergency relief from a real solution; audition for survival frames crowdfunding as a performance judged by popularity
The system takes credit for a kindness it did not provide, exposing the gap between the appearance of generosity and its absence
Defines charity and justice in contrast to give the argument a conceptual frame
Balanced opposing clauses sharpen the difference between what is chosen and what should not have to be asked for
Blurring the two leads to invisibility for some and false proof for others
Repeating works and worked turns the short denial into a qualified admission that still indicts the arrangement
The blunt four-word sentence after a long one delivers the verdict with finality
Moves from analytic argument to intimate exhortation addressed directly to donors
Speaks directly to readers who gave, honoring and redirecting their generosity at once
Remember... Remember also pairs the tender memory with the structural indictment
Qualifies the blunt denial by admitting it worked for her for a while, keeping the argument honest

tone_shifts.to: intimate, direct exhortation to the readers

blueprint.counterargument: Defenders of crowdfunding pages say the money is real and the comfort is real, and that donors do something good; the writer concedes both fully, then argues that a lifeboat is not a harbor and that the system has merely outsourced its stinginess to neighbors.

planned_flaws.flaw: The admission that Lenore would have disliked the column slightly risks undercutting the writer's authority to speak for her
planned_flaws.repair_type: The following sentence recovers by grounding the exhortation in her own documented behavior rather than her presumed opinion

provenance.note: Entirely fictional tribute column; all names, places and figures invented.

input.title: The Number Seven Bus
paragraphs: Lenore Quist drove the number seven bus for the Pell's Landing schools for twenty-two years and never once left a child at the curb because the clock said she could.
She kept a shoebox of spare mittens under the driver's seat.
She knew which kids needed a louder good morning and which needed none at all.

When she died last Tuesday, at fifty-eight, of the kidney disease that had been chasing her for two years, the town did what towns do: it brought casseroles, lowered the flag at the depot, and opened the fundraising page one more time to see the final figure.
Fifty-three thousand, four hundred dollars.
I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath.
The page went up in March of last year, built by her niece at the kitchen table while Lenore protested from the next room that she did not want her face on the internet.
The niece won.
The photograph showed Lenore in her reflective vest, one hand on the folding door, grinning at someone out of frame.

Within nine days the page passed its first goal; within a month it had covered the share of dialysis the insurance would not, the gas to a clinic forty miles away, and three months of rent she lost when she could no longer sit behind the wheel.
People she had driven as six-year-olds, now with mortgages of their own, wrote notes beneath their donations.
One simply said: you waited for me in the snow.
Here is the part the eulogies have skipped.
Four streets over lived a man named Aurelio Dansk, a night-shift machinist with the same disease, the same clinic, and the same forty-mile drive.
His page, which his daughter built with the same template, raised eleven hundred dollars.
He was not less sick, and he was not less deserving, unless we have quietly decided that deserving means being known, being photographed well, and having driven half the county's children to school.
He was simply a man whom fewer people had met, and the arithmetic of charity is pitiless about that.
I will concede what the defenders of these pages say, because it is true: the money was real, and so was the comfort.
Lenore read every note aloud, and her niece told me that on the worst mornings the page was the first thing she opened, before the pill organizer, before the coffee.
Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely.
But a lifeboat is not a harbor, and we should stop describing the boat as though it were the shore.
A system in which the sick must audition for their own survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to the kindness of neighbors and then taken credit for the kindness.
There is an old distinction worth reviving here, between charity and justice.
Charity is what one person chooses to give; justice is what no person should have to ask for.
When we blur the two, letting the warmth of the first stand in for the absence of the second, we make the Aurelios of the world invisible and the Lenores into proof that the arrangement works.
It does not work.
It worked for her, for a while, because she was a story that was easy to tell, and even that was not enough in the end.
So here is what I would ask you to remember, you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred.
Remember the mittens, the snow, the grin at the folding door.
Remember also that you were asked, out of your own pockets and on nine days' notice, to do something that should never have fallen to you at all.
Lenore would have disliked this column; she hated being made an example of.
But she waited for every child, including the ones nobody else was watching for, and I can think of no better instruction for the rest of us.

items.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: pay tribute to Lenore Quist while using the contrast between her campaign and a neighbor's to argue that crowdfunding exposes a failure that donors should not mistake for a solution
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening promises both to honor the figure and to tell the truth about it; paragraphs 3 through 5 build the argument that the system has outsourced its stinginess, and paragraph 6 asks donors to remember both Lenore and that the burden should never have fallen to them.

options.text: celebrate the generosity of a small town whose donations covered dialysis, travel and rent for a woman who had spent twenty-two years looking after its children
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This captures only paragraph 2; the writer explicitly moves beyond the eulogies in paragraph 3 and argues that the kindness, though lovely, is not the point.

options.text: persuade readers who donated to Lenore's page that their money would have been better directed toward less visible patients such as Aurelio Dansk
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer says nobody who gave did anything wrong and never asks readers to redirect donations; the argument is that no one should have had to be asked at all.

options.text: recount the stages of a long illness, from diagnosis to the loss of work to the final months, so that readers understand what kidney disease costs a family
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Details of the illness appear only as background in paragraph 2; the passage's organizing concern is the ethics of the fundraising, not the medical narrative.

items.stem: The detail that Aurelio Dansk's page "raised eleven hundred dollars" in paragraph 3 is offered primarily as evidence for the claim that

options.text: crowdfunding distributes help according to how widely a person is known rather than according to how sick or deserving that person is
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer stresses that Aurelio had the same disease, clinic, drive and template, then concludes he was simply a man whom fewer people had met; the figure isolates recognition as the deciding factor.

options.text: fundraising pages built by family members with a standard template are less effective than those assembled with professional help and better photographs
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The passage notes the same template precisely to rule out design as a difference; nothing suggests professional help was involved in either campaign.

options.text: night-shift workers in the county tend to have smaller social circles than public employees and therefore receive less support when they fall ill
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer does not generalize about occupations or social circles; the comparison is between two individuals, and the explanation offered is simply that fewer people had met him.

options.text: Lenore's niece showed unusual skill in choosing a photograph that made her aunt's campaign more appealing than a typical page
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Although the photograph is described in paragraph 2, Aurelio's total is not used to praise the niece; it is used to indict the arithmetic of charity.

items.stem: Which of the following sentences best states the central claim of the passage?

options.text: "A system in which the sick must audition for their own survival is not generous; it has outsourced its stinginess to the kindness of neighbors and then taken credit for the kindness."
options.label: correct
options.why: This sentence, arriving after the concession, is the position the comparison in paragraph 3 builds toward and the definition in paragraph 5 explains; the closing exhortation restates it in personal terms.

options.text: "I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath."
options.label: partially_right
options.why: This sentence announces the tension the column will explore and previews its dual purpose, but it states a difficulty rather than the argument's conclusion.

options.text: "Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely."
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: This is part of the concession to the defenders of crowdfunding; the writer grants it before pivoting with But to the actual claim.

options.text: "Lenore Quist drove the number seven bus for the Pell's Landing schools for twenty-two years and never once left a child at the curb because the clock said she could."
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: This is the opening anecdotal detail that establishes character; it supports the tribute but makes no argument about crowdfunding.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 4 and paragraph 5?

options.text: Paragraph 4 concedes the real benefits of the page before declaring the system inadequate, and paragraph 5 supplies a distinction that explains why confusing those benefits with a remedy causes harm
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 4 moves from concession to the lifeboat metaphor and the central claim; paragraph 5 then defines charity and justice and shows that blurring them makes the Aurelios invisible, giving the claim its conceptual grounding.

options.text: Paragraph 4 condemns the donors for mistaking a boat for the shore, and paragraph 5 softens that condemnation by admitting that the arrangement did in fact work for Lenore
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 4 explicitly says nobody who gave did anything wrong, and the admission in paragraph 5 that it worked for her for a while is immediately qualified as not enough, not a retraction.

options.text: Paragraph 4 defines the terms the argument depends on, and paragraph 5 applies those terms to the specific cases of Lenore and Aurelio introduced earlier
options.label: reversal
options.why: The definitions of charity and justice appear in paragraph 5, not paragraph 4; the order of the two functions is reversed.

options.text: Paragraph 4 presents the view of crowdfunding's defenders, and paragraph 5 introduces new evidence about Aurelio Dansk that refutes that view
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 5 adds no new evidence about Aurelio; it refers to the Aurelios of the world as a category and works by definition rather than by fresh example.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the writer develops the discussion of Aurelio Dansk primarily through

options.text: comparison of two closely matched cases, which allows the writer to isolate recognition as the one factor that explains the difference in outcomes
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph lists what Aurelio shared with Lenore (disease, clinic, drive, template) and then names the single difference, that fewer people had met him; the matched comparison makes the conclusion about charity's arithmetic feel earned.

options.text: narration of Aurelio's illness and his daughter's efforts, which deepens the reader's sympathy for a patient the eulogies ignored
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The paragraph gives almost no narrative of Aurelio's illness; it withholds story deliberately, and its aim is analytic rather than sympathetic.

options.text: classification of patients into those who are well known and those who are not, which lets the writer propose a fairer system of allocating aid
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The writer works with two individuals rather than categories here, and no alternative system of allocation is proposed anywhere in the passage.

options.text: a cause-and-effect sequence showing that Lenore's successful campaign drew donations away from Aurelio's and left him with less
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The paragraph does explain why Aurelio raised less, but it never claims Lenore's page took money from his; the cause named is simply that fewer people knew him.

items.stem: In the sentence beginning "A system in which the sick must audition" in paragraph 4, the semicolon primarily serves to

options.text: bind the rejection of the word generous directly to the correction that replaces it, so the second clause reads as an immediate verdict on the first
options.label: correct
options.why: The semicolon joins the negative judgment (is not generous) and the positive account (has outsourced its stinginess) without a conjunction, so the substitution lands at once rather than as a separate afterthought.

options.text: introduce a pause that softens the accusation against the system by giving readers a moment to absorb the writer's concession
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The concession ended in the previous sentences; this sentence is the rebuttal, and the semicolon tightens rather than softens the accusation.

options.text: separate the items in a list of the system's failures, each of which the writer has documented in the preceding paragraphs
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The semicolon joins two independent clauses, not list items; the clause that follows is a single claim with its own subject and verbs.

options.text: signal that the second clause reports what the defenders of these pages say, which the writer has promised to concede
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The defenders' view was stated and conceded earlier with a colon; the clause after the semicolon is the writer's own indictment, not reported speech.
